statement: What is the value of $1 \cdot 1! + 2 \cdot 2! + 3 \cdot 3! + \cdots + 9 \cdot 9!$? (Here $n! = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdots n$, so for example $4! = 24$.)

choices.misconception: I saw that the first sums 1, 5 and 23 sit just below 2, 6 and 24 and answered $10!$, forgetting that each sum is exactly one less than a factorial.
I found that each sum is one less than a factorial, but I used the factorial of the last number, 9, instead of the next number, 10.
I took $9!$ out of every term as if each factorial were $9!$, and was left with $1 + 2 + \cdots + 9 = 45$.
I thought the earlier terms were too small to matter and kept only the last term, $9 \cdot 9!$.

hints: Work out the sum with just one term, then with two, three and four terms.
The first few sums are 1, 5, 23 and 119. Compare each one with a nearby factorial. To trust the pattern, look for a way to write $k \cdot k!$ as a difference of two factorials.
Each sum is one less than a factorial: $1 = 2! - 1$, $5 = 3! - 1$, $23 = 4! - 1$, $119 = 5! - 1$. Also $k \cdot k! = (k + 1) \cdot k! - k! = (k + 1)! - k!$.

solutions.reliable: Try small cases: $1 \cdot 1! = 1$, then $1 + 4 = 5$, then $5 + 18 = 23$, then $23 + 96 = 119$. These are $2! - 1$, $3! - 1$, $4! - 1$ and $5! - 1$, which suggests that the sum up to $n \cdot n!$ is $(n + 1)! - 1$. To prove it, write $k \cdot k! = (k + 1) \cdot k! - k! = (k + 1)! - k!$. Then the sum is $(2! - 1!) + (3! - 2!) + \cdots + (10! - 9!)$, and everything cancels except $10! - 1! = 10! - 1$. The transferable idea: small cases suggest the pattern, and a short argument confirms it before you commit.
solutions.elegant: Add 1 to the sum and watch it collapse: $1 + 1 \cdot 1! = 2 = 2!$, then $2! + 2 \cdot 2! = 3 \cdot 2! = 3!$, then $3! + 3 \cdot 3! = 4!$, and so on, until $9! + 9 \cdot 9! = 10!$. So the sum is $10! - 1$.

whyOnTest: Nine factorials are too big to add by hand in a contest; four small cases reveal the pattern, and a one-line identity proves it.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
